title: Is Backpropagation Optimal? When Synthetic Gradients Improve Sample Efficiency
claim: A multi-layer computation path can be reinterpreted as a time-evolving state machine with local observations and a feedback signal.
layout: 2 panels, left-to-right, large arrow labeled 'layer steps as time steps'
description: The figure has two panels joined by a large gray block arrow labeled 'layer steps as time steps'. The left panel, 'Layered Computation', shows a grid of circular nodes in columns V_1, V_2, V_3, ..., V_L, with faint gray arrows between neighboring columns. One path is highlighted in black through the black nodes x_1, x_2, x_3 and x_L. Dashed arrows skip ahead to x_L, and gray-shaded nodes mark local observations. The right panel, 'Time Evolution', shows the same path as a horizontal chain of black circles x_1, x_2, x_3, ..., x_L at times t=1..L. Gray rounded squares z_2, z_3 and z_L sit below the chain with arrows pointing up into it. A dashed arrow skips across time, and a curved arrow labeled g_L points into x_L. The eye goes first to the black path and then to the arrow between the panels.
caption: From a network path to a state evolution trajectory. Left: a single path through a layered network is highlighted in black. Right: after treating layer steps as time steps, the same path is viewed as the trajectory of a state machine. The local observation zt includes node variable xt−1 by default. Shaded nodes denote local observations available at each step. Dashed arrows indicate information that skips across time. Curved arrow indicates a vectorized feedback gL.
abstract: Backpropagation is the default learning rule for artificial neural networks and is often treated as the settled approach whenever differentiability is available. In this work, we revisit this convention through a theoretical lens of sample efficiency. We introduce a unified vectorized feedback framework for loss-based and reward-based learning on computational graphs, in which synthetic gradients emerge as a natural alternative to backpropagation. We characterize the conditions under which synthetic gradients can achieve a lower gradient-estimation mean squared error than backpropagation. We construct examples illustrating that this sample efficiency advantage can be arbitrarily large. Experiments on contextual bandits and reinforcement learning tasks demonstrate the potential of our theoretical findings.
